anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statements or transaction patterns that process or return more data, touch rows inefficiently, or hold transactions open longer than business logic requires. 
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions acquire incompatible locks on the same resources, leading to long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall commit progress. 
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream replicas cannot receive, persist, or apply the primary’s log stream fast enough, causing widening replay lag and retained logs on the primary. 

When these three root causes strike together, the database exhibits a compound failure mode: heavy, inefficient SQL keeps transactions open for extended durations and enlarges their lock footprints; this inflates lock-wait queues and deadlock frequency while simultaneously generating large volumes of redo. The resulting commit delays propagate to the replication layer, where already backlogged apply threads fall further behind, increasing replica lag, growing on-disk log retention, and degrading read-scalability and failover readiness. End-user sessions experience highly variable and often excessive latency, frequent timeouts or deadlock retries, and eventually encounter stale reads or read-only routing failures on replicas. Operations teams observe surging lock-wait metrics intertwined with escalating replication delay and disk-space alerts, making it difficult to attribute slowdowns to a single subsystem.

Causally, inefficient workload logic expands the number of rows scanned or updated per transaction, which 1) locks more objects and for longer durations, intensifying lock contention, and 2) emits larger transaction logs that replicas must ship and apply. The prolonged blocking further postpones commits, causing bursts of log generation once locks are released; replicas receive these bursts in uneven waves they cannot keep up with, amplifying lag. Conversely, apply-side delays on replicas can hold replay locks that feed back into longer primary-side lock retention during synchronous or semi-synchronous commit protocols, reinforcing the contention. This feedback loop ties application-layer inefficiencies, lock-manager saturation, and replication pipeline overload into a single, self-amplifying composite anomaly that can spiral into severe throughput collapse and availability risk if not addressed.

entry.official_definition: Terminates any session that has been idle, but not within an open transaction, for longer than the specified amount of time.
entry.trigger_condition: A session is idle and not inside an open transaction longer than the configured threshold.
entry.workload_impact: The session is terminated; the documentation warns about using this with connection pools or middleware.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
